subtitle: Non-apparent disabilities are a reminder that appearance is incomplete information. Learn to respect a person’s privacy and respond to the relevant task and the need they have stated.
scope: For DHS staff in everyday workplace communication and collaboration. Original practice cases support learning about non-apparent disabilities; they do not diagnose a person, decide legal coverage, approve an accommodation or determine a real complaint. Employment accommodation and reporting use the actual agency procedures. Public-service access and any clinical or program records have their own applicable responsibilities; this staff course does not replace them.
introTranscript: Some disabilities are not readily visible. A person’s appearance, successful work or comfort during one activity does not tell us everything about the effort involved or a barrier in another activity. This course helps staff separate observation from assumption, respect privacy and respond to a relevant need without demanding a personal explanation. You will work through practice interactions involving information, timing and participation. The goal is useful understanding and practical judgment, not identifying which colleagues have a disability. Keep reflection private if you wish, use the practice cases and move at your own pace. No disclosure of your own or another person’s health information is required.

lessons.title: Separate what you see from what you assume
lessons.summary: An ordinary appearance or successful result does not reveal every barrier, effort or disability-related need. Notice the actual task without diagnosing the person.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an observable event from an unsupported conclusion about disability or effort.
objectives: Distinguish an observable event from an unsupported conclusion about disability or effort.
Explain why appearance and a completed result are incomplete information about a person’s experience.
Prepare a respectful task-focused response without asking a colleague to prove a diagnosis.
takeaways: A work result does not reveal every effort or barrier.
Ask about the task rather than assign a diagnosis.
lessons.statement: You can take a stated difficulty seriously without deciding what condition a person has.

image.caption: Colleagues participate in a shared activity; the photograph does not establish anyone’s health or access needs.

intro.heading: A visible moment is not the whole experience
intro.body:
In this example, during a DHS project, Finn contributes a carefully prepared written comparison. Later, Finn asks for the decision questions in writing because the rapid spoken discussion is difficult to follow. A colleague thinks, “The written work was excellent, so there cannot be a real difficulty.” That conclusion adds information the colleague does not have. Preparation, effort and the way information is presented can differ between tasks.

Non-apparent disability describes a disability that is not readily visible to someone else. The term is useful for questioning appearance-based assumptions; it is not a separate legal test or a way to diagnose colleagues from a list of behaviors. Physical, sensory, cognitive and mental-health-related conditions can involve needs other people do not immediately notice. This does not mean every hard meeting, quiet response or preferred method indicates a disability.

The current employment regulation distinguishes an achieved outcome from how a major life activity is limited. A successful result does not by itself settle a person’s experience or legal coverage. Finn’s completed comparison therefore should not be used as a test that cancels the stated difficulty in the later conversation. The course also cannot establish Finn’s eligibility or the effective accommodation from that example.

Separate three questions: what happened, what am I inferring and what useful information is relevant to this task? “Finn requested the questions in writing” is an event in the practice case. “Finn is exaggerating” is an unsupported interpretation. “Which decision information needs to be available during this discussion?” is a practical question. This distinction gives a colleague a constructive role without making them the investigator of another person’s health.

A response such as “Let us make sure the questions and relevant instructions are available through the appropriate process” addresses the shared work. If the person states a disability-related employment need, use the actual accommodation route rather than treat a peer’s agreement as an official decision. If there is an urgent safety or service concern, retain its actual response procedure; respectful uncertainty does not mean ignoring a known duty.

For learning, use Finn’s practice situation or a private example. You do not need to disclose a condition, identify another employee or submit proof that you changed a real practice. Understanding the difference between an observation and an inference is valuable in its own right.

inThisLesson: Recognize the limits of appearance and outcomes.
Respond to the actual task and stated need.
lessons.keyStatement: A visible result can tell you what was completed without telling you every barrier involved.

flashcards.back: A disability that is not readily visible to others. This description is not a diagnosis or an additional eligibility test.
The relevant event you actually know, such as a person asking for decision questions in writing.
An interpretation added to the event, such as assuming a successful writer cannot experience difficulty with rapid spoken information.
A response that examines the relevant information, method or process without requiring a personal health explanation from a colleague.

accordion.heading: Examine the leap in the practice case

items.title: The result is genuine, and the difficulty can be genuine
items.body: Finn’s careful comparison does not need to be discounted to recognize that another information method can be difficult. Treating these as competing facts forces an unnecessary choice. A colleague can respect the contribution and respond to the later request. What remains unknown should remain unknown instead of being filled with a judgment about credibility.

items.title: A visible aid is not a prerequisite for respect
items.body: Someone may use an aid you recognize, use a less visible support, or have no aid in that situation. None gives a colleague permission to determine the whole person’s capacity. In the practice case, a requirement to display a recognizable device would add a test unrelated to the actual information need. Use the appropriate process when a formal question must be resolved.

items.title: Curiosity can be directed toward the work
items.body: The useful question is which decision information must be available and how the person can participate in the task. Asking what diagnosis explains the request moves into private information without helping the peer do their assigned work. A person may choose to share some experience, but the course does not make that sharing the price of a respectful response.

tabs.heading: Three readings of the same moment

tabs.label: What is known
tabs.body: Finn finished the written comparison and later requested written decision questions. Those events concern different activities, so neither cancels the other. A task-focused note can preserve both without labeling the person. This lets the team examine the information method instead of argue over whether the person’s visible success makes a later request legitimate.

tabs.label: What is assumed
tabs.body: “Excellent written work proves there is no difficulty” treats a result as complete knowledge of effort and every other task. That can lead a colleague to dismiss the stated need before the proper process can examine it. The opposite guess, assigning a particular diagnosis because of the request, is also unsupported. Neither inference supplies an appropriate response.

tabs.label: What can be done
tabs.body: Identify the relevant questions, information and participation route within your role, and connect a stated disability-related need with its actual process. This may support the discussion while formal questions are handled. It is different from promising a particular accommodation or demanding medical evidence yourself; practical attention and proper responsibility can coexist.

check.question: Finn’s written comparison is strong, but rapid spoken questions are difficult. What can a colleague reasonably conclude?
check.correct: The completed result does not settle the later difficulty; respond to the relevant task without diagnosing or dismissing Finn.
wrong: Strong written work proves no disability-related barrier can exist.
The request proves a specific diagnosis that the colleague should record.
Finn must show a visible aid before the team can respond respectfully.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The two events do not establish a diagnosis or disprove a barrier. Task information and the appropriate process provide a constructive response.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A successful result does not reveal every effort or need in another task. Assigning a diagnosis turns a request into unsupported health information. Demanding a visible aid adds an appearance-based test rather than address the stated difficulty. Keep known events separate from these assumptions.

sorting.heading: Sort the response to Finn’s request

items.text: Finn asked for the decision questions in writing.
Finn cannot have any barrier because the report was completed.
Identify the questions the discussion needs to address.
The request proves a diagnosis to put in a team note.
Finn prepared a written comparison.
Use the actual employment accommodation route for a stated disability-related need.

lessons.next: Next, consider why a person’s experience may differ across situations or over time without turning that variation into a credibility test.

scenario.context: In this example, a colleague notices Finn chatting comfortably before a meeting and then questions why Finn requested written discussion questions.
scenario.prompt: Which response best fits the information available?
options: Tell Finn the comfortable conversation disproves the request.
Recognize that the activities differ, address the task information and preserve the appropriate request process.
Tell the team Finn must have the condition the colleague suspects.
responses: A casual conversation and a rapid decision discussion need not make the same demands. One does not settle the other.
This keeps the response useful without a diagnosis or an appearance test. Formal questions still use their actual process.
A peer’s guess is not established health information and should not become a team explanation.

lessons.transfer: Privately compare one practice observation with two possible interpretations. Identify which interpretation goes beyond what is known; no personal example or disclosure is needed.

move.control: Choose language that names the event and relevant task.
move.failure: The response turns a completed result or appearance into proof about an unknown condition or motive.
move.next: If useful, practice one task-focused sentence using Finn’s case and leave health details out.

lessons.title: Understand variation without testing credibility
lessons.summary: A person may experience different barriers in different activities or at different times. Variation is not a reason for coworkers to invent a test of who deserves support.
lessons.objective: Explain why one comfortable activity does not establish how a different task affects a person.
objectives: Explain why one comfortable activity does not establish how a different task affects a person.
Describe the current employment rule’s episodic or remission principle without determining an individual case.
Choose a task-focused response to a changed stated need while preserving actual work and safety responsibilities.
takeaways: Different tasks can make different demands.
An episodic condition is not judged only by a comfortable moment.
Changed needs belong in the relevant process, not a peer credibility test.
lessons.statement: Understanding variation means allowing for information you do not have, while attending to the task you do have.

image.caption: Participation in one activity does not show how a person experiences every other activity.

intro.heading: Avoid making one moment the standard for every moment
intro.body:
In another practice project, Mika completes a short morning conversation comfortably. During a longer session later, Mika says the format and length are creating difficulty and asks to discuss an adjustment through the appropriate route. A peer says, “You were fine this morning.” The statement may describe an impression, but its implied conclusion does not follow. Duration, activity, environment and a person’s experience can differ.

Some conditions are episodic or in remission. The current ADA employment regulation provides that such an impairment is a disability if it would substantially limit a major life activity when active. This principle prevents a comfortable moment from being the entire legal lens. It does not turn a peer’s observation into an assessment, diagnose Mika or establish that a specific request must be approved. The actual facts and authorized process still matter.

Distinguish variation from inconsistency in a story that needs investigation through assigned duties. A colleague’s role in ordinary collaboration is not to collect photographs, compare social activities or demand that the person demonstrate difficulty in public. Those activities can misread different contexts and intrude on privacy. Where an actual performance, safety or complaint issue requires examination, use the real procedures and authorized roles; the course does not prohibit assigned investigations.

Respond to the current task. What is the required activity, what difficulty has been stated and which responsible route can consider the need? Do not promise that an adjustment removes every duty. Equally, do not make “everyone uses the same method” the whole answer when the actual method may be what needs examination. A fair response preserves the relevant work requirement and the opportunity to consider effective participation.

Variation also applies to follow-through. A method that was useful for one task may need another look when the task changes. Discuss the work issue rather than speculate that a person has stopped trying or recovered because they appeared comfortable earlier. Not every change is disability-related, and staff should not decide that question from the learning example.

For this exercise, compare the two practice activities and list the facts still unknown. You can understand the conceptual distinction without offering a health story, making a legal determination or changing an actual schedule. Choose a private reflection or example if that supports your learning.

lessons.keyStatement: A person’s experience in a short conversation cannot establish their experience in a longer or different task.

flashcards.back: The activity, information, duration and environment relevant to a stated difficulty. Context helps frame a work question; it does not establish a diagnosis.
The current employment rule examines substantial limitation when the impairment is active, rather than treating a symptom-free moment as the whole question.
An improvised demand that a colleague visibly prove a disability or reproduce difficulty. It does not replace the authorized process.
A newly stated or altered task barrier that deserves the appropriate response, rather than an inference drawn from earlier comfort.

items.title: Duration can change the activity
items.body: A short exchange and a long session are different tasks in the practice case. Recognizing that difference does not guarantee that the requested change is the right answer. It prevents an invalid shortcut: using the short activity to dismiss the longer one before examining its actual demands. Describe both activities and the unresolved question instead of trying to settle the person’s health from the contrast.

items.title: Social activity is not a workplace assessment
items.body: A photograph from an unrelated activity may have none of the relevant information about its duration, support or effort. It cannot supply the individual work assessment the team has not done. Do not create a peer collection of such evidence. Assigned HR, accommodation or safety responsibilities have their proper procedures; ordinary curiosity does not confer those roles.

items.title: Actual duties remain meaningful
items.body: Taking a changed need seriously does not mean any requested option automatically replaces an essential duty. The responsible process considers the work and possible effective response. That is why both the dismissal and the blanket promise miss the point: each decides before the relevant inquiry. A staff member can preserve the task and connect the question to the proper role.

tabs.label: Dismissal
tabs.body: “You were comfortable earlier, so nothing can be difficult now” treats an earlier impression as a universal result. In Mika’s practice situation, the duration and format differ. Dismissal can stop a relevant question from reaching the process that should examine it. It also places the peer in a role they do not have: deciding the person’s experience from a moment they observed.

tabs.label: Automatic exemption
tabs.body: “Any changed need removes every work requirement” grants an outcome the conversation has not established. A useful adjustment concerns a particular task and actual circumstances. Keeping requirements and possible supports distinct permits the responsible process to examine effectiveness rather than forcing a choice between total dismissal and total exemption. The course does not approve either extreme.

tabs.label: Relevant response
tabs.body: “Let us identify the task difficulty and connect it with the appropriate process” preserves the current issue without a health judgment. Relevant work information can help the authorized role examine options. This response is not a promise about approval or timing; it recognizes that the peer’s comparison of two moments cannot settle the question and directs attention where it can be addressed.

check.question: Mika appeared comfortable in a short conversation but later reports difficulty in a long session. What is the sound response?
check.correct: Recognize the different contexts, address the stated task issue and use the appropriate process without deciding coverage or an accommodation from appearance.
wrong: Require Mika to reproduce symptoms publicly before the request can proceed.
Assume any changed need automatically removes every work duty.
Use the comfortable morning as proof that the later need is false.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Context and episodic variation prevent an appearance-based shortcut, while actual responsibilities and formal decisions remain with their proper roles.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Public reproduction of difficulty is an improvised proof demand that can intrude on privacy. Automatically removing all duties decides an outcome without the actual work and accommodation inquiry. Using morning comfort to reject a later need ignores different activities and the episodic principle. A relevant task question avoids all three shortcuts.

items.text: The morning activity lasted a few minutes; the later activity was a long session.
Mika must publicly demonstrate symptoms for coworkers.
Bring the stated work barrier to the actual accommodation route.
Comfort this morning proves no later difficulty can exist.
The task’s format changed between the activities.
Preserve actual emergency procedures for an urgent safety issue.

lessons.next: Next, examine what a colleague needs to know for collaboration and what information belongs in a private or formal process.

scenario.context: A practice peer proposes collecting Mika’s social photographs to decide whether the long-session difficulty is credible.
options: Use the photos as an unofficial medical assessment.
Announce that no actual work issue may ever be reviewed.
Avoid the peer surveillance, identify the relevant task issue and use the actual authorized process for any formal question.
responses: The photographs do not establish the task experience and peer curiosity does not authorize a health assessment.
Actual assigned work, safety and investigation responsibilities remain. The problem is an improvised peer assessment, not every authorized inquiry.
This preserves privacy and relevant responsibilities without treating a comfortable activity as proof about another context.

lessons.transfer: Privately identify two different demands in Mika’s practice activities. Name what remains unknown rather than assigning a health explanation.

move.control: Attend to relevant context and the actual stated need.
move.failure: A peer turns comfort, social activity or fluctuating difficulty into a diagnosis or a public proof requirement.
move.next: If useful, rehearse a neutral task question and the appropriate next process step using the practice case.

lessons.title: Respect privacy without treating it as suspicious
lessons.summary: A colleague can coordinate work without knowing another person’s diagnosis. Privacy and useful task information are different questions.
lessons.objective: Distinguish operational information from a private health explanation in a practice collaboration.
objectives: Distinguish operational information from a private health explanation in a practice collaboration.
Explain why voluntary sharing with one person does not establish permission for unrelated redistribution.
Prepare a respectful response to coworker curiosity while retaining actual confidentiality and reporting responsibilities.
takeaways: Private information is not the price of collaboration.
A limited disclosure is not permission for unrelated sharing.
Coordinate relevant work without inventing or broadcasting a reason.
lessons.statement: The information needed to coordinate a task may be much narrower than the explanation a curious colleague wants.

image.caption: A shared activity does not reveal who has chosen to disclose personal information.

intro.heading: Keep the person’s story separate from the team’s task
intro.body:
In a team in this example, Jae uses a different arrangement for part of a review. Pat asks a colleague what diagnosis explains it. The team may need to know the handoff time, where to send a question or who covers a particular task. That does not mean coworkers need Jae’s medical explanation. Guessing a diagnosis or asking Jae to justify the arrangement publicly does not improve the handoff.

For employment accommodation, MMB Policy 1433 protects medical information and the fact of a disability-related accommodation within its applicable confidentiality limits. Operational instructions can be communicated by the appropriate role without satisfying coworker curiosity about the private reason. Authorized need-to-know handling is different from a general team announcement. The policy’s documentation and confidentiality roles remain applicable; a course exercise cannot authorize access to another employee’s information.

A person may choose to share an experience with a colleague. Listen to the scope of that choice. “I wanted you to understand this situation” is not automatically permission to retell it in orientation, a team chat or a public program example. Ask before an optional reuse and follow the actual agency information requirements. Consent alone is not a substitute for any applicable protected-data or record-handling obligation. Do not invent a universal rule that nobody may ever discuss their own condition.

Privacy should not be treated as proof of dishonesty. A person may wish to discuss the work barrier with the responsible role rather than share details with peers. That choice does not tell you that the arrangement is unfair or the condition unreal. Similarly, someone who shares freely is not a spokesperson for everyone with a named condition. Respect the individual choice without building a group profile from it.

A useful peer response to Pat might be, “We can follow the handoff instructions without knowing someone’s private health information.” If the question involves a formal concern or a known duty, use its actual route instead of either gossiping or promising absolute secrecy. Required reporting, assigned investigations and appropriate emergency responses are not replaced by an informal agreement.

In this lesson, practice with Jae’s practice case. Keep personal reflections unrecorded if you prefer. No learner needs to reveal a condition, explain an arrangement or identify a coworker in order to understand the distinction.

inThisLesson: Understand the scope of voluntary sharing.
lessons.keyStatement: A relevant work instruction does not require a peer to know or announce the personal reason behind it.

flashcards.back: The task, timing, coverage or route people need to coordinate work. It does not automatically include a diagnosis.
Under the actual policy, medical information and disability-related accommodation status have restricted handling and applicable need-to-know limits.
What a person chose to share, with whom and for what purpose. A limited conversation does not establish unrelated reuse permission.
Personal learning that can remain unrecorded and undisclosed. It is valid without becoming an employee example for the program.

accordion.heading: Resolve the useful question, not the curiosity

items.title: The handoff may need an answer
items.body: If Pat does not know where to send an urgent review question, find the authorized handoff route. That need should not be dismissed as gossip merely because a different arrangement exists. Separate the missing operational instruction from the demand for a diagnosis. This gives the team a clear task response without exposing the private basis for an arrangement.

items.title: A public defense can still disclose
items.body: A colleague may want to protect Jae by telling everyone the health explanation. Good intent does not make that disclosure necessary or permitted. A response can protect the person’s privacy and address the team’s coordination issue without confirming an accommodation status. The appropriate role handles any actual confidentiality question and the information needed for implementation.

items.title: Absolute secrecy is not a promise to improvise
items.body: An informal promise never to share anything can conflict with a required report, authorized process or urgent response. Explain the appropriate boundaries rather than encourage exposure or promise more than your role allows. Private learning examples remain private by choice; actual work information still follows its applicable rules.

tabs.label: Useful coordination
tabs.body: The practice team needs the correct destination for a review question and the actual handoff timing. Those details let colleagues perform their roles. The appropriate instruction can be clear without identifying a health condition or inviting a vote on an individual arrangement. If the route is unclear, repair that work information instead of making personal disclosure the solution.

tabs.label: Coworker explanation
tabs.body: Pat’s curiosity about a diagnosis asks for a different kind of information. It may feel like an explanation of fairness, but broadcasting the reason does not establish whether the work process is appropriate and can violate applicable confidentiality. A peer should not fill the gap with a guessed diagnosis. Direct an actual policy question to its responsible role while keeping necessary task information available.

tabs.label: Chosen personal sharing
tabs.body: Jae may voluntarily tell a friend about an experience. The friend can respect that conversation without turning it into an orientation story or evidence about a whole group. An optional request for reuse should be separate from the original conversation, and actual information requirements still apply. Listening to a person’s chosen scope supports trust without pretending every disclosure is forbidden or every retelling permitted.

check.question: A coworker wants Jae’s diagnosis to explain a different work arrangement. What is the appropriate peer response?
check.correct: Use the relevant operational instructions and respect the personal information’s actual confidentiality boundaries rather than guess or demand the reason.
wrong: Announce the suspected diagnosis to defend Jae against criticism.
Treat Jae’s choice not to discuss health with peers as proof of dishonesty.
Promise absolute secrecy about every future issue regardless of applicable reporting duties.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Coordination does not automatically require personal health information. Privacy should coexist with the actual process and responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Announcing a guessed diagnosis adds speculation and may expose information rather than defend privacy. Treating private choice as dishonesty draws a conclusion it cannot support. Promising absolute secrecy ignores actual required reporting or authorized process boundaries. Address the task and follow the applicable handling instead.

items.text: The authorized route for a time-sensitive review question.
A guessed diagnosis added to a team chat.
Not telling peers a diagnosis proves the arrangement is dishonest.
The relevant coverage instruction from the responsible role.
The confidential fact of a disability-related accommodation.
No report will ever be made under any circumstances.

lessons.next: Next, consider how an initial request can be recognized without special words or a coworker medical review.

scenario.context: Jae privately shares an experience with one colleague. The colleague wants to use the story in an orientation session without asking.
options: Keep the original sharing scope distinct, seek any optional reuse permission separately and follow the actual agency information requirements.
Assume one private conversation permits every public reuse.
Declare that Jae is never allowed to speak about a personal condition.
responses: This respects the original choice without making consent alone an exception to protected-information requirements.
The original conversation does not establish an audience or purpose beyond what Jae chose.
People can choose personal sharing. The issue is another person’s unsupported redistribution, not a universal ban on self-expression.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice case, separate one coordination question from one unnecessary personal question. Keep the exercise private and do not collect another person’s health details.

move.control: Use only the relevant information for your role and its actual handling requirements.
move.failure: Personal curiosity, a guessed diagnosis or an absolute secrecy promise replaces the relevant task or formal responsibilities.
move.next: If useful, practice a response to Pat that provides the work route without confirming a private health explanation.

lessons.title: Recognize a request and connect it with the right process
lessons.summary: An initial disability-related employment request does not require a legal phrase or a form. Recognize the need while leaving documentation and decisions with the authorized roles.
lessons.objective: Identify an initial disability-related employment request in ordinary language.
objectives: Identify an initial disability-related employment request in ordinary language.
Distinguish prompt routing and appropriate later documentation from a peer or supervisor medical-information demand.
Choose a clear next response without promising an accommodation or treating consultation as a required gate.
takeaways: Ordinary words can begin the process.
Use the actual decision and documentation roles.
lessons.statement: A clear next step can help without forcing a person to become an expert in policy vocabulary.

image.caption: Participants in a shared discussion may use different ways to communicate a need.

intro.heading: Respond to what the person is asking
intro.body:
In a practice exchange, Jae tells a supervisor, “Because of a health condition, I need the detailed instructions in writing as well as spoken.” The supervisor says only a completed ADA form can count as a request. MMB Policy 1433 permits an initial request in different forms without particular legal words. The statement needs recognition and the actual prompt response, even though later process documentation may be needed.

The person receiving a request must promptly forward it to the appropriate decision-maker and tell the requester who that is. This is not a direction to forward a colleague’s personal story casually to everyone. Use the actual agency process and appropriate information handling. Agency delegation determines which decisions a supervisor or manager may make; this practice course does not establish DHS’s delegation or invent a named contact.

An employee can ask an appropriate role for a change without already knowing which exact accommodation will work. The process considers the work and effective options. Conversely, an ordinary preference without a stated disability-related need is not automatically a legal accommodation request. If clarification is needed, discuss the relevant work and available route rather than demand a diagnosis from peers or treat uncertainty as a reason to ignore a stated need.

Documentation questions have defined roles. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation from an applicant or employee seeking accommodation; appropriate questions belong to the ADA Coordinator. The policy does not allow medical records to be requested or accepted as accommodation documentation. Relevant documentation through that process is different from a full file, and initial recognition is different from a blanket promise that no later documentation can ever be needed.

A useful first response could be, “Thank you for explaining the work need. I will use the appropriate process and let you know who handles the decision.” It does not require a public demonstration, name a condition or guarantee approval. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant can provide guidance and feedback about relevant equity practice, but optional consultation does not replace the accommodation roles or become a prerequisite for using them.

Practice the response with Jae’s practice words. Learning does not require submitting an actual accommodation request or providing medical information. In real work, the policy and agency procedure govern the next step; the course’s short response is preparation rather than certification that the process is complete.

inThisLesson: Explain an actual next route clearly.
lessons.keyStatement: Recognize the initial need without creating a vocabulary test or an unauthorized medical review.

flashcards.back: Communication that asks for or states a needed change because of a medical condition; under the actual policy, no special phrase is required.
The role with actual authority under the agency’s procedure and delegation, not whichever colleague is most available.
For employment accommodation, appropriate medical-information requests belong to the ADA Coordinator, not a supervisor, manager or curious peer.
Guidance and feedback that can help staff develop equity practice without replacing mandatory processes or deciding an accommodation.

accordion.heading: Keep recognition, documentation and decision distinct

items.title: A request can be clear before the paperwork
items.body: Jae’s ordinary sentence links a needed work change to a health condition. Requiring the legal phrase first would create a gate the policy does not set for an initial request. Later written processing can still be appropriate. This sequence matters because “no special initial form” and “no documentation ever” are different claims; neither a barrier nor an unsupported exemption should be added.

items.title: Prompt routing needs a usable explanation
items.body: Forwarding through the actual process should include telling the person who handles the decision. Otherwise a referral can feel like the need disappeared into an unknown destination. The recipient should not invent a contact or promise a deadline. The useful contribution is an accurate route and appropriate handling, not a decision outside their authority.

items.title: Work questions are not a medical file request
items.body: Which instructions are difficult to follow and what result the task requires can help explain the work. A demand for a full health file seeks different information and does not belong to a supervisor or peer accommodation review. Use the coordinator for any appropriate documentation question. This protects the process without pretending that relevant work facts or later authorized documentation never matter.

tabs.heading: Three distinct parts of the response

tabs.label: Recognize
tabs.body: The first response notices the disability-related work need in Jae’s ordinary words. Recognition avoids a legal-vocabulary test and allows the actual process to begin. It does not determine whether the requested method is effective or approved. Keeping this step distinct prevents staff from confusing respectful receipt with a formal promise or with permission to ask for a diagnosis.

tabs.label: Route and clarify
tabs.body: The recipient uses the appropriate decision path and tells Jae who will handle the question. Relevant work information can clarify the task, while medical documentation remains with the coordinator under the actual policy. This is different from passing the story around the team or sending Jae to optional consultation as a gate. The route should preserve both prompt handling and the person’s information boundaries.

tabs.label: Decide and implement
tabs.body: Authorized roles examine the actual request and effective response under applicable requirements and procedure. A peer’s preferred option, coworker vote or short course exercise cannot make that decision. If a response is approved, provision and effectiveness still need their appropriate follow-through. Distinguishing these later questions prevents an initial conversation or a referral email from being reported as completion of the whole request.

check.question: Jae states a needed change because of a health condition without using ADA vocabulary. What is the sound first response?
check.correct: Recognize the initial request, use the actual prompt forwarding and notice process, and leave medical documentation and decisions with their appropriate roles.
wrong: Ignore the statement until Jae uses a legal phrase and completes a form.
Have the supervisor request Jae’s full medical records to verify the need.
Promise the exact adjustment is approved before the authorized process examines it.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Ordinary language can begin the process. Prompt handling can coexist with appropriate later documentation and formal decision responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A legal-phrase or form gate misstates the initial-request rule. A supervisor request for medical information or full records violates the policy’s accommodation-documentation role and limits. An automatic approval decides effectiveness and authority before the responsible process. Recognize and route the need without imposing or promising these extra steps.

sorting.heading: Identify the part of the request process

items.text: Jae states a needed change because of a health condition.
The recipient tells Jae who the appropriate decision-maker is.
Only the word ADA can begin the request.
The coordinator considers whether relevant documentation is appropriate.
A peer guarantees the exact accommodation before review.
Authorized roles examine which response will be effective for the actual task.

lessons.next: Next, connect shared collaboration practices with individual participation without treating one as a substitute for the other.

scenario.context: In this example, a staff member says all requesters must first discuss the issue with the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant, then wait for permission to approach the accommodation process.
options: Keep that gate because any consultant advice is mandatory.
Use the actual accommodation route; optional consultant guidance can support equity learning without replacing or delaying the proper process.
Let coworkers decide the request by a vote instead.
responses: A program resource cannot create a prerequisite absent from the actual procedure.
This preserves both useful consultant support and the actual accommodation responsibilities.
A coworker vote does not supply decision authority or an appropriate documentation process.

lessons.transfer: Privately rehearse a first response to Jae’s practice request. State the relevant route without naming an invented contact, promising approval or seeking health details.

move.control: Recognize the initial communication and follow the actual responsibilities.
move.failure: A vocabulary test, consultant gate or unauthorized medical request delays the appropriate response.
move.next: If useful, compare your practice response with the direct policy’s initial-request and forwarding sections.

lessons.title: Make collaboration useful without a diagnosis requirement
lessons.summary: Shared information practices can support participation. They do not diagnose staff, guarantee universal access or close an individual request.
lessons.objective: Compare a shared work-information practice with an individual employment accommodation process.
objectives: Compare a shared work-information practice with an individual employment accommodation process.
Choose a practical collaboration response that does not require a diagnosis or assign a group profile.
Explain why a pleasant interaction or a delivered feature does not by itself establish meaningful participation.
takeaways: Relevant shared practices can help the work.
An individual need still uses its actual process.
Check the task rather than infer success from politeness.
lessons.statement: Improve the shared task without making someone disclose a condition to justify ordinary clarity.

image.caption: People can participate through different methods without the image identifying their needs.

intro.heading: Support the work, preserve the individual process
intro.body:
A practice project discussion has no written decision questions and changes topics without identifying the action under consideration. Several participants ask for clearer information. One person has also made a disability-related employment request. The team wants to add written questions, but a colleague says that change will prove the individual request is solved. The shared action and the individual process are related, yet not interchangeable.

A team can examine the task information it provides: what decision is being considered, what material is relevant and how participants can contribute within the actual work procedure. An agenda or written question may improve clarity for the task. Its usefulness should not depend on persuading a particular person to reveal a diagnosis. It also should not be described as a clinically prescribed response for everyone with a named condition.

A person’s preference and experience can inform the relevant discussion without representing a whole group. Some participants may want written information; others may need a different arrangement or encounter a barrier the shared revision does not address. Avoid saying that non-apparent disabilities all need one method. Work from the actual task and person’s stated need, with the appropriate process for any formal question.

A delivered document is one action. Meaningful participation concerns whether the relevant information and contribution route can be used for the actual activity. Someone’s thank-you may show appreciation without showing that every part worked. Silence may leave feedback unknown. Examine the specific task rather than invite a general assurance such as “Everyone is happy now.” Use appropriately authorized methods and do not collect diagnoses to make the evaluation appear rigorous.

The individual accommodation process should not be closed merely because the team changed its meeting template. Conversely, a private individual adjustment need not be explained to every coworker to justify the broader information practice. Keep the responsible owner of a shared tool or instruction connected with the relevant work question while preserving the private request’s actual decision and confidentiality arrangements.

For practice, describe what the practice written questions change and what remains unexamined. A person may learn from that contrast privately, without preparing a real meeting, proving personal improvement or identifying anyone who needs support. In actual work, required accessibility, service and employment responsibilities remain in force beyond this optional course exercise.

inThisLesson: Examine participation rather than general satisfaction.
lessons.keyStatement: A shared improvement can be useful without proving that every person’s need has been met.

flashcards.back: The information or method used by a team for its common task. Its actual owner and responsibilities still matter.
A particular disability-related employment need considered through the proper accommodation process, not settled by a general template change.
The action of making a feature or resource available. It does not by itself show its effectiveness for the person and task.
Relevant information about whether the actual work or participation route can be used. Gratitude and silence answer different questions.

accordion.heading: Connect the two without merging them

items.title: Ordinary clarity need not demand personal disclosure
items.body: The practice team can identify its decision questions because the task needs them. It does not need a public list of diagnoses to justify explaining the work. This gives the shared improvement a relevant purpose and leaves personal choice intact. It also avoids pretending that a useful general practice is a diagnosis-specific treatment or automatically satisfies every applicable access requirement.

items.title: A template change may leave an individual question open
items.body: The request could concern an aspect of participation the new questions do not resolve. Keep the actual request with its responsible process rather than mark it complete because the general team action occurred. This allows the shared improvement to be useful while leaving its limits visible. The two questions may inform each other without having the same decision-maker, evidence or information boundaries.

items.title: Different feedback means different evidence
items.body: “Thank you for sending the questions” confirms appreciation or receipt in the practice exchange. It does not establish that the person could contribute to the decision. A relevant follow-up may examine the actual task through an appropriate process. If no response is available, the result is unknown; it is not proof of universal success or failure. Avoid turning a polite exchange into an outcome claim.

tabs.heading: Compare the shared and individual questions

tabs.label: The shared revision
tabs.body: Written decision questions can make the task clearer for the practice group by showing which choices are under discussion. Describe that purpose and what was actually made available. A clearer document remains only part of the participation path: delivery, use and other relevant requirements may need examination. This claim is narrower and more useful than announcing that a new template made the meeting accessible to everyone.

tabs.label: The individual process
tabs.body: An employee’s stated disability-related need concerns that person’s actual task and circumstances. It may include a question the shared revision does not answer. The authorized accommodation process examines effective options and retains appropriate confidentiality. A general team change cannot decide the request, and coworker approval cannot replace its actual decision. Connecting useful work information should not expose the private basis for an arrangement.

tabs.label: The evidence of use
tabs.body: The relevant question is whether the person could obtain the decision information and contribute through the actual route. A receipt or thank-you shows something different. State what was checked and what remains unexamined, without diagnosing staff or inferring group results from a single response. This gives the team a practical basis for a next review while avoiding either universal reassurance or a presumption that all missing feedback means failure.

check.question: The team sends written questions and receives a thank-you. What can it accurately say?
check.correct: The questions were provided and appreciated in that exchange; their task effectiveness and any individual request still need their appropriate examination.
wrong: The thank-you proves every person’s access need is met.
The template change automatically closes every individual accommodation request.
Collect diagnoses from all participants to prove the shared revision worked.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Describe the action and the actual feedback without inflating either into a universal or individual process result.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A thank-you does not establish every task outcome or every person’s access. A template change cannot decide the individual accommodation process. Collecting diagnoses introduces unnecessary private information instead of examining the relevant work route. Use the appropriate task evidence and retain the separate responsibilities.

sorting.heading: Keep the claim proportionate
categories: Shared action or relevant task evidence

items.text: The written decision questions were sent through the relevant route.
items.category: Shared action or relevant task evidence

items.text: The authorized role reviews a remaining individual participation need.
One thank-you proves universal access.
The team checks whether the actual contribution route was usable through an appropriate method.
items.category: Shared action or relevant task evidence

items.text: A coworker vote closes an accommodation request.
The private request keeps its actual confidentiality and decision roles.

lessons.next: Next, use what you have learned for proportionate follow-through while retaining the separate reporting and request responsibilities.

scenario.context: A practice project owner improves the shared meeting document. The owner wants to announce the private condition of the employee whose need prompted discussion.
options: Announce the condition because any general improvement requires a personal explanation.
Stop the shared improvement because it might also help that person.
Explain the shared task purpose without exposing private accommodation information, and preserve the individual request’s proper process.
responses: The task can justify the work-information improvement without broadcasting a private health explanation.
A useful shared revision need not be abandoned merely because it may also support an individual.
This connects the common work and individual process while respecting their different information and decision boundaries.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice meeting, name one useful shared action and one question it cannot settle. Keep the reflection private or discuss only the invented task.

move.control: Describe the actual action and relevant evidence, with the individual process still intact.
move.failure: A shared feature, polite response or guessed group need becomes proof of universal or individual completion.
move.next: If useful, prepare a proportionate practice statement: what changed, what was examined and what remains open.

lessons.title: Follow through without making the person a project
lessons.summary: Useful follow-through attends to the actual task and process, preserves privacy and reporting duties, and leaves room for private personal learning.
lessons.objective: Prepare a proportionate follow-through response to a practice unresolved task barrier.
objectives: Prepare a proportionate follow-through response to a practice unresolved task barrier.
Distinguish optional learning and peer support from mandatory accommodation or reporting responsibilities.
Identify when evidence is missing without inferring success, diagnosis or motive.
takeaways: Do not delay required processes for informal reassurance.
Private learning is valuable without a public success story.
lessons.statement: Continued attention should help the work and respect the person, rather than turn every interaction into a health review.

image.caption: Working together does not require coworkers to disclose or evaluate one another’s personal health.

intro.heading: Keep attention proportionate and responsibilities clear
intro.body:
In the final practice case, Jae says the supplied instructions still do not resolve an aspect of the review task. A colleague wants to ask for fresh medical proof, while another wants to call the issue closed because the document was delivered. Neither response follows the relevant question. Jae has described a remaining work barrier; the appropriate process can examine effectiveness without an improvised peer health review.

Follow-through distinguishes a decision, provision and actual usefulness. A process email may show that a decision occurred. Delivery shows that something was provided. Whether the person can perform the relevant activity with that response is a further question. Staff should bring an unresolved task issue to its actual responsible role rather than diagnose the cause, approve a new arrangement themselves or demand health records.

Respectful peer support can include listening, using the appropriate work instruction and avoiding speculative explanations. It does not make the person an ongoing object of observation. Do not record a colleague’s appearance, attendance at social events or disclosure choices as a casual profile of credibility. A real performance, safety or investigation responsibility still follows its actual procedure and authority; the course does not remove it.

A separate protected-class concern has its own route. Under MMB Policy 1436, employees are strongly encouraged to report such incidents through the stated routes. Managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. An informal apology, a peer conversation or optional consultant advice does not delay that manager duty. Assigned investigation responsibilities remain with the actual procedures and authorized roles; this course makes no finding about a real case.

Where relevant feedback is missing, say so. Silence does not show that the arrangement is effective, that a disability has disappeared or that the person is dissatisfied. A proportionate next step uses the responsible task or request process rather than manufacture a story about motivation. The consultant can provide guidance and feedback as staff build capacity; staff retain their own work and actual responsibilities.

End with personal understanding if that is the useful result for you. You may privately reconsider a familiar assumption about appearance or variation without producing a work product or disclosing a personal experience. Use a practice case for optional practice. A learning completion is not certification that a real accommodation, complaint, service issue or formal equity analysis is complete.

inThisLesson: Preserve formal reporting and assigned authority.
Reflect privately on what remains unknown.
lessons.keyStatement: A useful next step addresses the remaining task through its proper role without inventing a health story or declaring unexamined success.

flashcards.back: Whether the response enables the relevant task or participation in the actual circumstances. A delivery receipt alone does not answer it.
A limit in what is known. It does not establish satisfaction, failure, recovery or motive.
The actual policy distinguishes strongly encouraged employee reporting from managers’ and supervisors’ immediate HR or agency Affirmative Action Officer reporting duty.
Attention to the relevant unresolved task and proper process, with privacy and actual assigned duties preserved.

items.title: A remaining barrier is not a new peer medical examination
items.body: Jae’s statement concerns the task. A peer can direct that question to the proper process without asking for proof or a whole history. Appropriate later documentation questions remain with the coordinator under the actual policy, not with a curious teammate. Keeping the distinction lets the work issue receive attention without making repeated disclosure the default cost of asking for a useful response.

items.title: Formal responsibilities do not depend on a friendly ending
items.body: An apology or a calmer team exchange can matter personally while a protected-class allegation still requires the actual response. For managers and supervisors, immediate reporting cannot wait for informal resolution. A peer is not required by this course to adjudicate the event or improvise an investigation. Use the applicable procedures, and preserve authorized assigned duties instead of either delaying them or inventing new ones.

items.title: Learning does not need another person’s story
items.body: A private reflection can reveal that you equated appearance with capacity or gratitude with task success. That is a meaningful learning result even if nobody else sees it. An optional practice sentence can help apply the insight. Do not collect a coworker’s personal information to demonstrate that you completed the course, and do not treat completion as proof that an actual work issue is resolved.

tabs.label: The task remains difficult
tabs.body: Jae identifies a specific part of the review that the supplied instructions do not resolve. Describe that task issue and bring it to its appropriate owner or request process. It is not evidence that Jae is ungrateful, exaggerating or unable to work generally. Relevant follow-through can examine the remaining barrier while keeping medical documentation and decisions with their proper roles.

tabs.label: A protected-class concern is raised
tabs.body: In this example, a manager hears an allegation that someone was excluded because of disability. That concern is not simply another meeting-format preference. The manager immediately reports through HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follows the actual procedure. Optional support or apology can coexist with that responsibility, but cannot be used as a wait-and-see prerequisite or a course-made finding of misconduct.

tabs.label: Feedback is not available
tabs.body: The team knows a document was supplied but has no relevant task feedback. It can accurately report provision and the unresolved evidence question. It cannot infer that every need was met, that the person recovered or that silence proves failure. Use an appropriate next review if needed; avoid turning the uncertainty into a private health narrative or collecting unrelated information to make a progress claim look complete.

check.question: The team has a delivery receipt but no relevant feedback about the task. What is the accurate conclusion?
check.correct: The resource was provided; its effectiveness remains unexamined, so use an appropriate next process step without inferring health or motive.
wrong: Silence proves the person has recovered and no longer needs support.
A receipt proves every task barrier and formal request is resolved.
Ask peers to obtain new medical records as a routine follow-up.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Provision and effectiveness are different questions, and missing feedback remains missing rather than supporting an invented outcome.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence cannot establish recovery or the absence of need. A receipt documents provision, not every task result or formal process completion. Peer collection of medical records is not an appropriate accommodation follow-up and violates the relevant role boundaries. State the known action and open task question, then use its actual responsible process.

items.text: Jae identifies the part of the review still difficult.
A manager immediately reports a protected-class allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer.
A receipt proves the person no longer has a disability-related need.
The responsible process examines whether the response works for the actual task.
An authorized role follows assigned agency investigation procedures.
Peers collect social photographs and health files to test credibility.

lessons.next: You can revisit the practice cases or use the job aid for an appropriate task. Private understanding is a valid learning result; real duties still follow the actual policies.

scenario.context: In this example, a manager hears an allegation that an employee was excluded because of disability. A teammate suggests waiting until an apology and consultant discussion are complete before reporting.
options: Immediately report the allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow the actual procedures; optional discussion does not delay that duty.
Wait for an apology to determine whether the allegation matters.
Use the course to decide a real violation and impose an unassigned punishment.
responses: This preserves the manager’s actual reporting responsibility and authorized procedures without a learning or consultant gate.
Informal resolution is not a prerequisite for the manager’s immediate report.
The course makes no actual-case finding or grant of authority. Assigned decisions and investigations remain with their real procedures.

lessons.transfer: Privately name one assumption you would now question and one appropriate responsibility you would preserve. A practice case is enough; no disclosure or real work product is required.

move.control: State what is known, what remains open and which actual role can address the relevant question.
move.failure: A delivery, apology or silence is treated as automatic completion, or peers replace the authorized process with health scrutiny.
move.next: If useful, keep a private practice note separating the task question, information boundary and responsible next route.

jobAid.subtitle: A practical reminder for ordinary work, with actual policies and roles still governing formal decisions.
remember: Appearance and completed work are incomplete information about another person’s experience.
Different activities and times can involve different demands; do not diagnose or test credibility from a comfortable moment.
Use relevant task information and actual processes without making personal disclosure a learning or collaboration requirement.
Optional course practice and consultant support do not replace accommodation, reporting, service or assigned investigation duties.

sections.heading: When a need is stated
items: Separate the event from your interpretation. Identify the relevant task and what remains unknown.
Recognize an ordinary-language initial disability-related employment request; later appropriate processing is a separate question.
Use the actual prompt forwarding and notice process. Do not invent a named contact, deadline, delegated decision or required consultant gate.

sections.heading: When privacy or medical information arises
items: Coordinate the work instruction without broadcasting a personal diagnosis or confidential accommodation status.

For accommodation documentation, supervisors and managers do not request medical information; appropriate questions belong to the ADA Coordinator. Agencies do not request or accept medical records as accommodation documentation.
Keep chosen sharing within its scope and follow actual information requirements for any reuse. Do not infer permission from a limited private conversation.

sections.heading: When following through
items: Distinguish decision, provision and effectiveness; report missing feedback as unknown rather than success, recovery or failure.
Keep a shared work-information improvement connected with, but distinct from, an individual request.

Preserve Policy 1436 immediate manager and supervisor HR or agency Affirmative Action Officer reporting for protected-class allegations or incidents. Retain actual authorized investigation and emergency responsibilities.
Use practice cases and private reflection for learning. No disclosure, real work product or universal access certification is required.
